Female Pacific staghorn sculpin reach an ultimate total length of 46 centimeters [Li = 46 centimeters], a size that places them among the larger members of the cottid family within their estuarine range. Field surveys conducted in San Francisco Bay indicate that sexual maturation commences when females attain a total length of approximately 20 centimeters [Lp = approximately 20 centimeters], marking the onset of active vitellogenesis. At this pubertal stage, individuals weigh roughly 121 grams [Wwp = roughly 121 grams], a body mass that reflects substantial somatic investment prior to the initiation of reproductive allocation. The transition from juvenile to mature status involves considerable gonadal recrudescence, and length-frequency distributions from gill-net samples confirm that few immature fish exceed this size threshold. Comparative data from related Cottus species suggest that the length at maturity in Leptocottus armatus is somewhat elevated relative to freshwater congeners, likely an adaptation to the variable salinity regimes and seasonal prey pulses characteristic of its brackish-water habitat. Growth trajectories derived from otolith increment analysis reveal that females typically require two to three growing seasons to achieve the 20 centimeter milestone.

Newly emerged larval Pacific staghorn sculpin are remarkably minute, with a recorded wet weight at birth of just 0.0023 grams [Wwb = 0.0023 grams], a value derived from the diameter of the adhesive demersal egg. This initial mass is consistent with the pattern observed in other cottids, where the yolk-sac larva remains entirely lecithotrophic for the first several days post-hatching. The tiny prolarvae drift within the water column, their transparent bodies and minimal energy reserves necessitating rapid development of feeding structures. Once the mouth opens and the yolk is fully absorbed, the exotrophic larva must encounter suitable microzooplankton prey within a narrow temporal window to avoid starvation. The extreme small size at emergence imposes a high risk of early mortality, but those individuals that successfully transition to exogenous feeding embark on a phase of accelerated growth. The initial mass of 0.0023 grams [Wwb = 0.0023 grams] stands in stark contrast to the adult body sizes that these larvae will ultimately achieve, underscoring the dramatic ontogenetic scaling that characterizes this species.

Adult females of Leptocottus armatus can attain a substantial body mass, with the ultimate wet weight for females reaching approximately 1640 grams [Wwi = approximately 1640 grams]. This value, derived from a length-weight relationship fitted to large individuals, represents the asymptotic size approached by the oldest and most fecund members of the population. At such masses, the females are typically in their sixth or seventh year and display the deep-bodied, robust morphology characteristic of senescent cottids. The allometric scaling exponent used in the estimation aligns closely with values reported for other benthic marine sculpins, reflecting the conservative shape changes that accompany post-maturational growth. Individuals approaching this ultimate mass contribute disproportionately to the annual reproductive output, as their larger body cavity accommodates a greater volume of developing oocytes. The contrast between the 121 gram [Wwp = 121 gram] mass at puberty and the 1640 gram [Wwi = 1640 gram] asymptotic mass illustrates the extensive scope for post-maturational growth that defines the life history strategy of this iteroparous species.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], the reproductive output of female Pacific staghorn sculpin has been quantified in terms of both clutch size and spawning frequency. Individual females produce approximately 30 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 30 eggs per clutch], and they complete roughly one spawning event each year [F_R_i = roughly one spawning event each year]. This annual reproductive schedule aligns with the species' temperate latitude, where a single extended spawning season in late winter is followed by a prolonged period of gonadal quiescence. The combination of modest clutch size and low annual event frequency results in a conservative lifetime fecundity, a pattern consistent with the production of relatively large, well-yolked eggs that give rise to the small but well-provisioned larvae described earlier. The 7 °C [T = 7 °C] thermal regime used in these observations mirrors the typical bottom water temperatures encountered by gravid females in their native estuaries during the peak spawning window, ensuring that the measured rates are ecologically relevant.

Maximum lifespan in Pacific staghorn sculpin has been documented at 10 years [am = 10 years], under the same thermal conditions of 7 °C [T = 7 °C] that characterize their deep-channel estuarine refugia. This longevity estimate, derived from mark-recapture studies and validated by otolith annulus counts, positions the species as a relatively long-lived member of the Cottidae when compared to freshwater sculpins of similar body size. The extended lifespan reflects a life history strategy characterized by delayed maturity, iteroparous reproduction, and substantial post-maturational growth, as evidenced by the 1640 gram [Wwi = 1640 gram] ultimate wet weight achieved by the oldest females. Senescence in this species appears gradual, with females in their ninth and tenth years still producing viable clutches, albeit with slightly reduced clutch sizes compared to prime-age adults. The consistency of the age estimates under the 7 °C [T = 7 °C] regime suggests that thermal conditions exert a strong influence on both growth rate and physiological aging in this cool-water adapted species.
